Solid State Physics · Properties of Solids

Module III — Semiconductor properties

Theory notes: concepts, results and what every symbol means

Intrinsic & extrinsic

in one lineA semiconductor is an insulator with a small band gap (about 1 eV). Heat breaks a few bonds and makes electron–hole pairs (intrinsic). Adding a trace of Group V or Group III atoms adds electrons or holes on purpose (extrinsic), and that is how every device is made.

What a semiconductor is

Put the three kinds of solid side by side by how well they conduct. Conductors have resistivities of –m, insulators –m and more, and semiconductors sit in between: to m. Ge and Si (Group IV) have resistivities of about 0.6 and m. Compound semiconductors come from Groups III–V (GaAs, InP) and II–VI (CdS).

The band picture from Module II explains the middle position: the valence band is full and the conduction band empty, exactly as in an insulator, but the gap between them is small enough for room-temperature heat to push a few electrons across.

Group IV element at 0 KAt room temperature
C (diamond)5.51 eVinsulator
Si1.16 eVsemiconductor
Ge0.75 eVsemiconductor
Sn (grey)0.08 eVconductor
Pb0conductor

Same column of the periodic table, same diamond-type bonding, and the gap shrinks steadily down the group. That single number decides insulator, semiconductor or conductor.

Two properties every exam asks for:

  • Negative temperature coefficient of resistance. A metal conducts worse when hot (more scattering). A semiconductor conducts better when hot, because heating makes new carriers faster than it slows the old ones.
  • Doping changes everything. Adding impurity atoms in a controlled way, about 1 in to , changes the conductivity enormously. The impurity takes the place of a host atom, so the crystal structure does not change.

The small gap also fixes the wavelength of light the material emits or absorbs: that is why semiconductors make LEDs, lasers and solar cells.

Intrinsic semiconductors

In pure Si each atom shares its four valence electrons in four covalent bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron (the diamond structure of Module I). Step through the bond picture:

At 0 K every electron is in a bond: pure Si is an insulator at 0 K. The valence band is full and the conduction band empty. Above 0 K a few electrons get enough thermal energy to break free. Each one leaves a hole, an empty place in a bond, which also carries current: a neighbouring bond electron can jump into it, so the hole moves the other way. One broken bond gives one electron–hole pair, so in a pure sample

Properties of a hole: charge ; it moves in the valence band, in the direction of the field; it is not a particle but the absence of an electron in an otherwise full band; it has a larger effective mass and smaller mobility than an electron, because it moves in a nearly full band under the applied field and the ionic field of the lattice.

Generation and recombination. Pairs are made all the time by heat. A free electron that meets a hole drops back into the bond, giving out about (often as light). In equilibrium the two rates balance:

wheregeneration rate: electron–hole pairs made per unit volume per secondrecombination rate: pairs lost per unit volume per secondconstant that depends on the materialelectron and hole concentrations of the pure crystal (equal)

where depends on the material (it is related to the densities of states at the band edges). Because the recombination rate is proportional to the product of the two concentrations, this balance is the first hint of the law of mass action, .

Extrinsic semiconductors

n-type (donors). A Group V atom (P, As, Sb) uses four of its five valence electrons in bonds. The fifth is held only weakly, so a little energy frees it. Its energy level, the donor level , sits in the gap just below : about 0.01 eV below in Ge and 0.03 eV in Si. Against eV at room temperature, almost every donor gives its electron to the conduction band and becomes an immobile positive ion. Electrons are the majority carriers, thermally made holes the minority carriers.

p-type (acceptors). A Group III atom (B, Al, Ga, In) completes only three bonds. It takes an electron from a neighbouring Si atom to complete the fourth, leaving a hole there. Its acceptor level is just above , about 0.01 eV. The impurity becomes an immobile negative ion; holes are the majority carriers.

How big is the effect? Si has atoms per . Doping at 1 in gives donors, against at 300 K: some 30 000 times more electrons than the pure crystal has, from one foreign atom in a hundred million.

learn this by heart

In both types the law of mass action holds: at a given temperature. Doping raises one carrier and lowers the other in proportion. The crystal stays neutral: .

where marks get lost

A donor atom does not make a hole when it gives its electron away: what it leaves is a fixed positive ion, not a mobile hole. Only broken Si–Si bonds make holes. Likewise an acceptor makes a mobile hole and a fixed negative ion, not a free electron.

Drift, mobility,

in one lineA field gives the carriers a small extra velocity on top of their random motion: . Electrons and holes both carry current, so . In a pure sample rises as , and against measures the gap.

Drift velocity and mobility

With no field the carriers move at random and give no current: for every electron going left there is one going right. A field accelerates electrons one way and holes the other, but they keep colliding (with vibrating atoms, impurities, defects) and lose the extra velocity each time. On average they gain a steady extra velocity, the drift velocity, proportional to the field:

wheredrift velocity: the average velocity gained from the fieldmobility: drift velocity per unit fieldapplied electric field

The constant is the mobility: drift velocity per unit field, in . It is the same idea as the Drude picture of Module II, with : a long time between collisions and a light effective mass make a mobile carrier.

Why electrons beat holes. A hole's motion is really a relay of bond electrons in a nearly full band, so it has a larger effective mass and collides more effectively: (Si: 0.048 against 0.135). That is why devices that use electrons (n-type channels) are faster and preferred.

Electrons and holes drift opposite ways but, having opposite charges, their currents add.

Drift and diffusion. Carriers also move down a concentration gradient (diffusion current). In a sample with uniformly spread impurities there is no gradient, so only the drift current counts here. The two are linked by the Einstein relation (0.026 V at room temperature).

Conductivity and temperature

Taking the mobilities as constant, all the temperature dependence comes from (derived in the next section): . The exponential swamps the , so a plot of against is very nearly a straight line, and its slope gives the gap. This is the standard laboratory way of measuring .

Metal against semiconductor, with impurities. Impurities in a metal add scattering, so its conductivity falls. Impurities in a semiconductor add carriers, so its conductivity rises, by many orders of magnitude, even though they also scatter a little. Temperature works the same way round: a metal's falls as , a semiconductor's climbs exponentially.

The recipe: states occupation

Every carrier count in this module is the same two-step recipe from Module II. How many places are there at energy (the density of states ), and what is the chance each is occupied (the Fermi function )? Multiply and add up over the band:

whereelectron concentration in the conduction bandhole concentration in the valence bandbottom of the conduction bandtop of the valence banddensity of states in each bandprobability that a state is filledprobability that a state is empty, that is, holds a hole

Two simplifications make the integrals easy. Near a band edge the band is parabolic, so is the free-electron with the effective mass. And because is several inside the gap, everywhere in the conduction band, so : the Fermi tail is a Maxwell–Boltzmann tail. Such a semiconductor is called non-degenerate.

Electrons in the conduction band

An electron at energy in the conduction band has kinetic energy . So the free-electron density of states applies with and . Near room temperature eV, much smaller than , so the Fermi function's tail is exponential.

Read the answer as "the band behaves like states all sitting at ". is the effective density of states: for silicon , and the Boltzmann factor says what fraction of those are filled.

Holes in the valence band

A hole is a state left empty, so count . Holes become exponentially rarer deeper in the valence band, the mirror image of the electrons.

whereconductivity of n-type materialelectron concentrationelectron chargeelectron mobilitydonor concentration (all ionised, so )
  1. A → B (about 10 K to 50 K), the ionisation region: rises as more donors are ionised; maximum when all are ionised.
  2. B → C (up to about room temperature), the extrinsic plateau: falls slightly: is fixed but the mobility drops as lattice vibrations grow. This is the working range of devices.
  3. C → D, the intrinsic region: steep rise: broken bonds (intrinsic carriers) overtake the donors, and the curve joins the intrinsic line.
